name: Despotism
summary: Despotism is a form of government in which a single ruler holds unlimited power. Montesquieu, the thinker who made the concept central to modern political thought, sets it against monarchy: the despot governs by his own will and caprice instead of fixed laws, rules alone or through one deputy, and tolerates no intermediate bodies. The defining sources describe how power is held and say nothing on economics, society or foreign policy.
scope: The general form of government the name stands for, as the Cambridge Dictionary defines it (rule by a ruler with unlimited power) and as Montesquieu's The Spirit of Laws, read through the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, analyses it as one of three types of government. It is audited as a family: answers come only from those definitions of the form, not from the policies of rulers called despots. Quesnay's legal despotism, enlightened absolutism, absolutism, autocracy and totalitarianism have separate entries or are other concepts, and their texts are not used.

notes: Themes searched: dictionary definition (Cambridge; Britannica Dictionary and Merriam-Webster refused access), the Stanford Encyclopedia's Montesquieu entry, and Montesquieu's Spirit of Laws (Books II, III, V, VI, VIII, XII-XIII, XIX search for despotic government). The sources define the form by who holds power and by what law binds him, so answers exist only on government-structure statements; Montesquieu's remarks on despots' effects on commerce, education, women or religion were not used because they describe consequences rather than a stated position. Critics' accounts are not evidence, and rulers called despots have no entry-level record here. Uncertainty-rule failure is the honest result.
